title: The Sasanian Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Sasanian Empire, from Ardashir’s round city and Shapur’s capture of a Roman emperor through Mani, the walls of Derbent, Khosrow I’s great arch and the books brought from India, to the last war with Rome, the Arab conquest, the death of Yazdegerd III and Ferdowsi’s Book of Kings.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Sasanian Empire, from about 224 CE to today
note: Based on Sasanian inscriptions and coins, on Roman and Byzantine historians (Ammianus, Procopius, Agathias and Theophanes), on Armenian and Syriac writers, and on Arabic and Persian histories written after the conquest, above all al-Tabari; each chapter says which it follows. The later histories mix record with legend. The site of al-Qadisiyyah is approximate. India lies beyond the map’s eastern edge, so a route runs off the map towards it. Native names are given in Latin letters. The map is stylised and not to scale. Lands under Powers are painted loosely.

steps.title: Ardashir’s round city
steps.text: In Persis (Fars), the homeland of the old Persian kings, a local ruler, Ardashir, builds a city laid out as a perfect circle about two kilometres across, with a fortress and palace nearby. He defies his Parthian overlord, Artabanus IV, and in 224 CE defeats and kills him at Hormozdgan. A new dynasty, named after his ancestor Sasan, begins.
steps.today: Today: the circle of Ardashir-Khwarrah is still clear from the air beside Firuzabad, Fars, Iran.

steps.title: Crowned by the god
steps.text: Below the tombs of the Achaemenid kings, Ardashir carves a relief: on horseback, he takes the ring of kingship from the god Ohrmazd (Ahura Mazda), while their horses trample his defeated rival and the evil spirit Ahriman. He calls himself king of kings of Iran (Eranshahr). Zoroastrian faith and kingship are now bound together.
steps.today: Today: Naqsh-e Rostam, about 6 km north of Persepolis, Fars, Iran.

steps.title: A Roman emperor captured
steps.text: Ardashir’s son Shapur I beats the Roman emperor Gordian III in 244 CE, and his successor Philip pays 500,000 denarii for peace. In 260 CE, near Edessa, Shapur captures the emperor Valerian, who dies in captivity. Shapur’s inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam boasts of it, and a relief there shows Roman emperors before him.
steps.today: Today: Şanlıurfa, Turkey. Shapur’s inscription is on the stone tower called the Kaaba of Zoroaster.

steps.title: Built by Roman captives
steps.text: Shapur settles tens of thousands of Roman prisoners in Iran, including engineers. They help build his new city, Bishapur, whose palace floors carry mosaics in Roman style. Tradition says Valerian’s men built the dam and bridge at Shushtar, still called Band-e Kaisar, “Caesar’s dam”. Captives also settle a new city, Gundeshapur, in Khuzestan.
steps.today: Today: the ruins of Bishapur, near Kazerun, Fars, Iran; some of its mosaics are in the Louvre.

steps.title: Mani, prophet of light
steps.text: Mani, born near Ctesiphon, teaches that the world is a battle between light and darkness, and Shapur lets him preach. Under Bahram I, pressed by the Zoroastrian high priest Kartir, Mani is imprisoned and dies, by tradition at Gundeshapur, in 274 or 277 CE. His faith, Manichaeism, spreads west to Roman Africa and east to China.
steps.today: Today: Shahabad, near Dezful, Khuzestan, Iran; little of Gundeshapur is left above ground.

steps.title: Shapur II and Julian
steps.text: Shapur II rules for seventy years, from 309 to 379 CE. In 363 the Roman emperor Julian marches down the Euphrates to Ctesiphon, cannot take it, and is killed by a spear during his retreat. His successor Jovian buys a safe road home by giving up Nisibis and lands east of the Tigris. The Christians of Nisibis move to Edessa.
steps.today: Today: Nusaybin, on the Turkish–Syrian border.

steps.title: Walls against the steppe
steps.text: Raiders from the steppe press on the empire’s north and east; in 484 CE King Peroz is killed fighting the Hephthalites (White Huns). The Sasanians build great walls: at Derbent, stone walls run from the Caspian into the mountains, and east of the Caspian the Wall of Gorgan stretches about 195 km. Excavations date both to these centuries.
steps.today: Today: Derbent, Dagestan, Russia. Its citadel and walls are a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Khosrow and the great arch
steps.text: Khosrow I, called Anushirvan, “of the immortal soul”, has already crushed the Mazdakites, who preached sharing property. As king he surveys the land for a fixed tax and pays a standing cavalry. At Ctesiphon stands the Taq Kasra, a palace hall under one of the largest brick vaults ever built; whether he or Shapur I built it is disputed.
steps.today: Today: the Taq Kasra still stands at Salman Pak, Iraq, though part of it fell in 1888.

steps.title: Khosrow’s better Antioch
steps.text: In 532 CE Khosrow and Justinian agree an “Eternal Peace”, Rome paying 11,000 pounds of gold. It lasts eight years. In 540 Khosrow sacks Antioch and carries its people to a new city near Ctesiphon. Procopius says he named it Khosrow’s Better Antioch and gave it baths and a hippodrome, where its people could watch chariot races.
steps.today: Today: Antakya, Turkey. The site of Khosrow’s new city, near Ctesiphon, has not been certainly identified.

steps.title: Books from India
steps.text: Khosrow welcomes learning: Greek philosophers, driven out when Justinian closes the Athens schools, join his court. The physician Burzoy brings the Panchatantra, Indian animal fables, and puts it into Middle Persian; through Arabic it becomes Kalila and Dimna. Tradition says chess came from India then too. Later writers tell of a great medical school at Gundeshapur; historians debate its size.
steps.today: Today: Shahabad, near Dezful, Iran. Iran’s Jundishapur University of Medical Sciences, in Ahvaz, takes its name.

steps.title: The fire of Adur Gushnasp
steps.text: Beside a deep spring-fed lake in the mountains burns Adur Gushnasp, one of the three great sacred fires of the Zoroastrian faith, linked to the warriors and kings. Later writers say kings came here as pilgrims and gave rich gifts. Clay seals found on the site name the fire, so archaeologists are sure this ruined walled temple is the place.
steps.today: Today: Takht-e Soleyman, West Azerbaijan province, Iran; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The last great war
steps.text: When the emperor Maurice, who had helped him to the throne, is murdered in 602 CE, Khosrow II goes to war with Rome. Persian armies take Antioch in 613 and Jerusalem in 614, carrying off the relic of the True Cross, then Egypt by 619. In 626 a Persian army and the Avars besiege Constantinople, but cannot take it.
steps.today: Today: Jerusalem. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, burned in 614, was rebuilt.

steps.title: Heraclius strikes back
steps.text: The emperor Heraclius strikes into Iran instead, and in 624 CE sacks the temple of Adur Gushnasp. In December 627 he wins at Nineveh. Khosrow II is overthrown and killed by his son in 628. Peace returns the True Cross, but the empire falls into chaos: about a dozen rulers in four years, among them two queens, Boran and Azarmidokht.
steps.today: Today: the mounds of Nineveh lie within Mosul, Iraq.

steps.title: Al-Qadisiyyah
steps.text: Arab Muslim armies, united under the caliphs of Medina, invade Iraq. At al-Qadisiyyah, near al-Hira, Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas defeats the Persian general Rostam Farrokhzad after days of fighting, and Rostam is killed. The capital, Ctesiphon, falls soon after, and the Taq Kasra is used for a time as a place of prayer.
steps.today: Today: the battlefield lay south-west of Kufa, Iraq; its exact site is not known.

steps.title: The victory of victories
steps.text: Yazdegerd III, the young king of kings, gathers a last great army in the Zagros mountains. At Nahavand in 642 CE the Arab armies defeat it; Arab historians call the battle “the victory of victories”. After it, Persian resistance breaks into separate provinces, and the Arab armies take the Iranian plateau city by city over the following decade.

steps.title: The last king of kings
steps.text: Yazdegerd III flees east from province to province. In 651 CE, near Merv, he is killed; al-Tabari’s best-known account says by a miller, for his rich clothes, though accounts differ. His son Peroz reaches Tang China and lives at the court in Chang’an. Many Zoroastrians later sail to India, where their descendants are the Parsis.

steps.title: The Book of Kings
steps.text: At Tus, the poet Ferdowsi finishes the Shahnameh (Book of Kings) in about 1010 CE: some 50,000 couplets in Persian, from the first mythical kings to Yazdegerd III. The Sasanian kings fill its last part. Persian survives conquest as a language of poetry and government, and Iranians still read the Shahnameh, and name their children from it.
steps.today: Today: Ferdowsi’s tomb at Tus, north of Mashhad, Iran.

items.name: Ardashir I
items.text: A ruler from Persis who overthrew the Parthians and made himself king of kings of Iran. Later Persian legend, in the Book of Deeds of Ardashir, tells of a humble shepherd’s son destined to rule; his inscriptions name his father Papak and his ancestor Sasan. He ruled with his son Shapur in his last years.

items.name: Shapur I
items.text: Shapur I beat three Roman emperors and took one captive, and recorded it in three languages at Naqsh-e Rostam. He settled Roman prisoners across Iran and let Mani preach at his court. Christian writers later claimed he used Valerian as a footstool; historians treat that as hostile legend.

items.name: Mani
items.text: Mani called himself the last in a line of prophets after Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus. He wrote his own scriptures and illustrated them, so that his faith would not be lost. Manichaeism was persecuted almost everywhere, yet lasted for a thousand years; Augustine of Hippo followed it as a young man.

items.name: Shapur II
items.text: Shapur II ruled for seventy years, one of the longest reigns known. Later tradition says the nobles crowned him before he was born. He fought Rome for decades, won back Nisibis after Julian’s death, and persecuted Christians, whom he suspected of siding with a Christian Rome.

items.name: Khosrow I
items.text: Khosrow I became the model of the just king in Persian and Arabic writing. He reformed taxes and the army, built walls and canals, sacked Antioch, sheltered Greek philosophers and had Indian books translated. His minister Bozorgmehr, a wise counsellor in later stories, may be mostly legend.

items.name: Khosrow II
items.text: Khosrow II, called Parviz, “the victorious”, won back his throne with Roman help, then came closer than any Persian king since Darius to rebuilding the old empire. His reign ended in defeat and his murder. His love for Shirin became one of the great Persian romances, told by Nizami.

items.name: Boran
items.text: Boran, a daughter of Khosrow II, was one of the few women to rule in her own name in Iran. In a short reign amid civil war she made peace with Rome and struck coins with her own portrait. Later Persian writers remembered her as just. Accounts of how her reign ended differ.

items.name: Yazdegerd III
items.text: Yazdegerd III was crowned as a boy, perhaps eight years old, in the chaos after Khosrow II. He spent his reign losing his empire, moving from city to city further east as the Arab armies advanced. Zoroastrians long counted their years from his accession, and some still do.
